items.title: [Windows][Desktop 26.1007.2314.0] Repeated 0x3B BSOD in nt!CmpKeySecurityIncrementReferenceCount during local execution

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: tool-calls
labels.description: Issues related to tool calling

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

26.1007.2314.0

### What subscription do you have?

Plus

### What platform is your computer?

Windows 11 Pro 26H2 x64, OS reports build 26300.9457.

### What issue are you seeing?

Codex Desktop local execution has triggered three `SYSTEM_SERVICE_EXCEPTION (0x3B)` BSODs over two days on a machine that had been stable for roughly two years.

Two kernel dumps independently confirm the same failure signature and the same Codex -> PowerShell -> Python execution ancestry. The third crash occurred **without visual/computer-control use**, so the issue is not limited to Codex computer-use / virtual mouse workflows.

I am not claiming Codex user-mode code is the kernel root cause. The crash occurs in Windows registry kernel code during `NtRenameKey`, so this may be a Windows kernel race/use-after-free or an interaction with a kernel/filter driver. However, Codex local execution is the repeatable trigger context in all observed crashes.

### Repeated crash signature

```text
Bugcheck:          SYSTEM_SERVICE_EXCEPTION (0x3B)
Exception:         0xC0000005
Failure bucket:    AV_nt!CmpKeySecurityIncrementReferenceCount
Failure hash:      {79c641f6-31cc-b664-22f7-c3c4625d9fe3}
Faulting function: nt!CmpKeySecurityIncrementReferenceCount+0x1c
```

WinDbg stack from the latest kernel dump:

```text
nt!CmpKeySecurityIncrementReferenceCount+0x1c
nt!CmpReferenceSecurityNode+0x54
nt!CmRenameKey+0xc7b
nt!NtRenameKey+0x3c2
nt!KiSystemServiceCopyEnd+0x28
```

At the fault:

```text
rip=fffff800ec0a2800
rcx=000001f1801a3d44

nt!CmpKeySecurityIncrementReferenceCount+0x1c:
mov dword ptr [rcx+0Ch],edx
```

The pointer is invalid/unmapped at the point of the access violation.

### Faulting process / ancestry

The latest dump initially reports `PROCESS_NAME: Registry` because the faulting thread is attached to the Registry process, but `!thread` shows the **owning process is python.exe**:

```text
THREAD ... Cid 6778.58ec
Owning Process   ... Image: python.exe
Attached Process ... Image: Registry
```

The process tree from the kernel dump is:

```text
ChatGPT.exe
└─ codex.exe
   └─ pwsh.exe
      └─ C:\Users\<user>\Desktop\Mastixa\WindowsReleaseSuppliers\build-venv\Scripts\python.exe
         └─ C:\Users\<user>\Desktop\Mastixa\WindowsReleaseSuppliers\psf-python-3.14.8\python.exe
            └─ faulting thread -> NtRenameKey -> CmRenameKey -> CmpKeySecurityIncrementReferenceCount
```

The exact image paths were recovered from `EPROCESS.SeAuditProcessCreationInfo.ImageFileName` in the kernel dump.

The faulting child `python.exe` had existed for only **2.201 seconds** at bugcheck time.

The previous kernel dump showed the same Codex / `pwsh.exe` / build-venv Python / PSF Python ancestry and the same registry-rename failure path.

### Timing from Codex session log

The last recorded Codex validation command completed successfully before the crash:

```text
...\build-venv\Scripts\python.exe ...\artifact_probe.py test_year_context_core
Ran 11 tests in 5.960s
OK
exit_code=0
completed at 23:12:08.160Z
```

The kernel dump records the bugcheck at:

```text
2026-10-10 02:12:26.843 UTC+3
```

So the prior test itself completed normally. A new Python child in the same Codex execution tree was then created shortly before the BSOD. I have not deliberately reproduced again because this is a full kernel crash.

### Crash history

- 2026-10-08: first `0x3B / 0xC0000005`, same `CmpKeySecurityIncrementReferenceCount+0x1c` registry-rename stack in minidump.
- 2026-10-09: second crash; kernel dump confirmed faulting Python in Codex -> pwsh -> venv Python -> PSF Python chain.
- 2026-10-10: third crash; same failure hash/function/stack and same process chain, **without computer-use/visual control**.

### Other dump observation

`!blackboxpnp` records this on the crashes:

```text
PnpProblemCode : 24
DeviceId       : VHF\HID_DEVICE_SYSTEM_VHF\9&2cafb34a&0&2_Slot00
```

On a normal boot the same VHF device is healthy (`CM_PROB_NONE`) and is a Microsoft VHF child under a Logitech POWERPLAY / G502 LIGHTSPEED receiver. I do **not** know whether this is causal or merely transient crash-time state.

### Environment notes

- Codex Desktop: 26.1007.2314.0
- Windows 11 Pro 26H2 x64, build 26300.9457
- Hyper-V present
- HVCI reported disabled in dump
- Python supplier: CPython 3.14.8
- Bitdefender installed
- Proton VPN / WireGuard components installed
- Logitech G HUB / POWERPLAY / G502 LIGHTSPEED present
- AMD GPU drivers present

These are listed as environment context only; I have no evidence that any specific third-party driver is the root cause.

### Expected behavior

Codex should be able to start and terminate local command subprocesses without causing a Windows kernel crash.

### Safety / reproduction note

I am intentionally **not** reproducing this again because it has already caused three BSODs. I have preserved:

- the latest kernel dump
- earlier minidumps/kernel-dump evidence
- WinDbg output
- the Codex JSONL session log around the crash
- exact process ancestry and executable paths

I can provide sanitized WinDbg logs and, if OpenAI has an appropriate private upload path, the kernel dump/session evidence.

### Related issue

This may be related in category to #40119 (Codex local command runner causing Windows `0x3B`), but the kernel failure is different. That report crashes in `win32kfull!SetMagnificationInputTransform`; this report consistently crashes in the registry path `nt!CmpKeySecurityIncrementReferenceCount -> CmRenameKey -> NtRenameKey`.

items.title: Transient diagnostics SQLite failure leaves permanent failed state and an opaque warning despite writer recovery

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: CLI
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex CLI

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

items.body:
## What issue are you seeing?

Codex repeatedly displays a generic diagnostic-log database warning during normal use. The message gives no failure category, and `codex doctor` reports healthy databases. A transient failure also permanently marks the writer as failed after persistence recovers.

Observed message:

> Codex couldn't save diagnostic logs to its local database. Use /feedback with logs included before closing Codex, or run `codex doctor` for diagnostics.

Environment: macOS 26.5.1, arm64; standalone `codex-cli 0.160.1`, Ghostty 1.3.2; other installed clients sharing the same Codex home included bundled 0.160.0 and daemon 0.162.1. No model request or account credentials are needed for the isolated reproduction below.

## Local evidence

Before cleanup:

- `logs_2.sqlite`: 103,186,432 bytes.
- `logs_2.sqlite-wal`: 700,956,232 bytes.
- 12 Codex processes had the log DB open, several for almost two days.
- `PRAGMA quick_check` returned `ok`; approximately 142 GiB of disk space remained.
- A passive checkpoint succeeded; the WAL's allocated file size alone did not establish corruption or an outstanding checkpoint blocker.

Deleting only diagnostic rows through SQLite, checkpointing, and vacuuming reduced the database to 40,960 bytes and WAL to zero. Ten existing process identities subsequently persisted fresh records successfully. Conversation databases, sessions, auth, and config were untouched. `codex doctor --summary` reported `state: databases healthy` and sufficient free disk space.

**The original SQLite failure category was not recovered.** Contention is a reproduced trigger, not a proven historical diagnosis for the original warning. The large WAL is an observation, not an established cause.

## Reproduction through the installed app-server

Tested using the installed standalone 0.160.1 binary with a fresh temporary `CODEX_HOME`, no copied config or credentials, and no model requests:

1. Start `codex app-server --listen stdio://` with the temporary home.
2. Send JSON-RPC `initialize` with `clientInfo: {name: "diagnostics-repro", version: "1"}` and `capabilities: {experimentalApi: true}`; wait for its successful response, then send `initialized`.
3. Connect to the temporary home's `logs_2.sqlite` using Python's `sqlite3` and execute `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` to hold the writer lock.
4. Send six `config/read` requests with empty params, keeping the writer lock for 18 seconds (long enough to cover the 10-second log flush interval and 5-second SQLite busy timeout).
5. Observe a `warning` notification with `threadId: null` and the exact message above.
6. Roll back the synthetic writer transaction. Send six more `config/read` requests and allow 12 seconds for another flush.

Observed result: the warning was emitted, then 116 diagnostic rows were successfully persisted after releasing the lock; `PRAGMA quick_check` returned `ok`. The entire test home was removed afterward. This reproduces the warning on a new, tiny database and demonstrates writer recovery without deleting the database.

## Source-level cause and diagnostic gap

Source inspected at release commit `d27764b82f7118f674371e6d6e76271d9d606edb` (`rust-v0.160.1`):

- [SQLite connection options](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/d27764b82f7118f674371e6d6e76271d9d606edb/codex-rs/state/src/sqlite.rs#L309): five-second busy timeout.
- [Log batch insertion](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/d27764b82f7118f674371e6d6e76271d9d606edb/codex-rs/state/src/runtime/logs.rs#L11): insert and partition pruning share a write transaction.
- [Flush failure handling](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/d27764b82f7118f674371e6d6e76271d9d606edb/codex-rs/state/src/log_db.rs#L529): a failed batch is consumed without retry; the error is classified and `has_write_failure` is set true. Successful later writes never clear it.
- [Failure reporter](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/d27764b82f7118f674371e6d6e76271d9d606edb/codex-rs/feedback/src/lib.rs#L200): the sanitized failure diagnostic goes exclusively to the process's bounded in-memory feedback ring, bypassing tracing. The public warning does not include even the safe category (`busy`, `locked`, `full`, etc.). A separate `codex doctor` process cannot read that ring.
- [In-process startup](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/d27764b82f7118f674371e6d6e76271d9d606edb/codex-rs/app-server/src/in_process.rs#L459): each newly created reporter re-emits the warning if the shared writer has ever failed, even after recovery. Deduplication is per reporter, not per writer lifetime. This is a source-level replay path, not a claim that the stdio reproduction emitted repeated notifications.
- [Existing recovery test](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/d27764b82f7118f674371e6d6e76271d9d606edb/codex-rs/state/src/log_db_failure_tests.rs#L64) explicitly demonstrates successful recovered writes while `has_write_failure()` remains true. [Feedback selection](https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/d27764b82f7118f674371e6d6e76271d9d606edb/codex-rs/app-server/src/request_processors/feedback_processor.rs#L518) also permanently falls back from persisted logs after any historical failure.

The permanent flag and in-process replay path are also present in the `main` files inspected during this investigation (main head reported as `4bad6d78e9b50f9fa8bd941f1db012ed491ad2da`). No claim is made that latest main was compiled or runtime-tested.

## Expected behavior

- Distinguish a transient log-write failure from continuing database failure, and communicate recovery when later writes succeed.
- Include the already-sanitized error category in the warning or expose a local read-only diagnostic path. Users should be able to identify the cause without uploading their entire feedback log buffer.
- Preserve historical lost-log information for feedback separately from current writer health; avoid replaying an old failure as a new warning when reattaching an embedded server.
- Consider bounded handling/retry of transient SQLite contention for diagnostic batches.

This report concerns the runtime warning, recovery state, and missing local diagnosis. It differs from #27741's startup-blocking large-log-database failure and from the existing TRACE/WAL growth reports.

### What issue are you seeing?

I’m signed into Codex CLI v0.162.0 with a Pro 500 account. Fast mode works, but Ultrafast doesn’t appear as an available option, and there is no /ultrafast command.

Type /ultrafast in the CLI's tui interface and/or run codex -m gpt-6.1-sol -c 'service_tier="ultrafast"'

- Model: gpt-6.1-sol

items.title: Report terminal program status with OSC 7501
items.body:
Report terminal program status with OSC 7501

## Why

Lifecycle status reporting was limited to direct iTerm2 sessions. OSC 7501 lets other terminals receive Codex's program state.

## What changed

- Emit OSC 7501 with `app=codex` and states `idle`, `working`, or `blocked` whenever stdout is a terminal, including multiplexed sessions. Report `blocked` when user action is required.
- Continue emitting iTerm2's OSC 21337 status and bounded activity details in direct iTerm2 sessions.
- Clear status before handing the terminal to an external program, as well as on suspension and exit, and re-emit the current state after returning.

## Testing

Add coverage for OSC 7501 encoding, combined iTerm2 output, clearing both protocols, and protocol selection across terminal and multiplexer environments. Update lifecycle tests and status snapshots for the new protocol.

items.title: Add observers for initial exec-server connection attempts
items.body:
Add observers for initial exec-server connection attempts

## What changed

Expose `Environment::observe_connection_attempts` and `ConnectionAttemptOutcome` to report elapsed time and success, failure, or cancellation for initial connections. Measure from the end of provisioning through client installation, including connection retries.

The first registered observer wins. Past attempts and reconnections are omitted.

## Testing

Extend tests to assert failure followed by success when startup is retried, and a single cancellation notification when an environment is replaced during startup.

items.title: Add opt-in gRPC over stdio for the code-mode host
items.body:
Add opt-in gRPC over stdio for the code-mode host

## What changed

- Add `grpc+stdio://` as a host transport and the disabled-by-default `code_mode_host_grpc` feature flag to select it.
- Share a lazy HTTP/2 channel and host process across code-mode sessions while keeping session state isolated.
- Use HTTP/2 keepalives to detect unresponsive hosts, kill and reap disconnected children, and spawn a fresh host on reconnect. Exit the host when its stdio connection closes.

## Testing

Add coverage for shared-host session isolation, host exit on stdin EOF, and recovery after an unresponsive host is reaped. Exercise nested tool calls with both legacy stdio and gRPC stdio, asserting that the feature flag selects the expected transport.

items.title: Explain session creation failures during server shutdown
items.body:
Explain session creation failures during server shutdown

## Why

Graceful shutdown rejects new sessions with an invalid-request error. Give clients a structured shutdown reason and show command center users why session creation is paused.

## What changed

- Add `data: {"reason":"serverShuttingDown"}` to app-server shutdown admission errors while retaining JSON-RPC code `-32600`.
- Show a dedicated shutdown message explaining the wait for active turns and automatic reconnection for non-embedded servers. Recognize older servers by their exact draining message only when error data is absent, and preserve retained-worktree cleanup guidance.
- Keep the command center reconnect presentation when a shutdown error covers the initial overview and no conversation is open.

## Testing

Extend admission and WebSocket shutdown assertions, add embedded and daemon shutdown message snapshots, and cover reconnection with a shutdown error over the initial command center.

items.title: [Linux desktop] Codex message submission hangs; new threads fail and app can remain on loading logo

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

labels.name: connectivity
labels.description: Issues involving networking or endpoint connectivity problems (disconnections)

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

items.body:
## Environment

- OS: Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS, x86_64
- App: ChatGPT Linux desktop package (`chatgpt`), version `26.1007.21434`
- Installation source: `https://persistent.oaistatic.com/codex-app-prod/linux/deb` (stable)
- Session: GNOME / X11 (Electron process arguments include `--ozone-platform=x11`)
- Product area: Codex inside the ChatGPT desktop app
- Observed: October 10, 2026
- Browser ChatGPT works normally on the same machine/account.

## Summary

Codex inside the Linux ChatGPT desktop app intermittently stops accepting messages. The send button spins indefinitely; existing conversations can still be opened, but sending a message and creating a new thread fail. If I close and relaunch the app, it can remain indefinitely on the animated OpenAI logo/loading screen.

The issue has recurred after a full system restart temporarily restored normal operation. Disabling GPU acceleration with `chatgpt --disable-gpu` did not resolve it. The installed version and APT candidate are both `26.1007.21434`.

## Steps to reproduce

The failure is intermittent; this is the sequence observed on the affected installation:

1. Launch the ChatGPT Linux desktop app and open Codex.
2. Use Codex normally for some time.
3. Send a message in a conversation.
4. Observe that the send button continues spinning and no response arrives.
5. Open another existing conversation: history can load, but sending messages still does not work.
6. Try creating a new thread: this also fails.
7. Close and relaunch the app. On the affected occurrence, it remains on the animated OpenAI logo/loading screen.
8. Restarting the whole system restored operation once, but the same failure recurred later.

## Expected behavior

Codex should accept a message and start a turn, and the user should be able to create a new thread. If a backend or IPC connection fails, the app should recover or display an actionable error instead of leaving the send button or startup animation spinning indefinitely.

## Actual behavior

- Message submission hangs with an indefinitely spinning send button.
- Existing conversation history remains accessible, but new messages and new threads fail.
- Relaunching can leave the app stuck on the animated OpenAI logo.
- ChatGPT in the browser works normally at the same time.
- `chatgpt --disable-gpu` did not fix the issue.
- A full system restart restored operation temporarily, but did not prevent recurrence.

## Diagnostics collected

### Process state

While the UI was stuck, the desktop main process, Electron renderer/GPU/network processes, and local Codex app-server were still present. The local app-server was:

```text
/usr/lib/chatgpt/resources/codex -c features.code_mode_host=true app-server ...
```

The app-server's parent was the main ChatGPT process. Sending `SIGTERM` to the app-server caused that PID to disappear; a new app-server process was subsequently observed under the still-running ChatGPT main process. This shows the app can respawn the app-server, but does not by itself establish that the app-server caused the original failure.

A separate remote Codex exec-server was also present; I did not terminate it.

### Journal output

The user journal contained:

```text
[IpcClient] Received broadcast but no handler is configured method=ipc-connection-reset
```

This appeared around the failure/relaunch period. The journal also showed the main frame finishing load, the window becoming ready to show, and the local app-server successfully initializing on a prior launch.

Other messages included Chromium zygote `Broken pipe (32)` errors when launching a new instance while another browser session was already running, and an Electron AudioContext warning. These may be incidental and are not asserted as the root cause.

A separate Orbit messaging diagnostic showed an authenticated request returning HTTP 200, but that request was not identified as the failed Codex message-send operation; it should not be taken as proof that the failing request succeeded.

### Package version

```text
Installed:  26.1007.21434
Candidate:  26.1007.21434
```

No newer package was available from the configured stable APT repository when checked.

## Suspected area (unconfirmed)

The symptoms suggest a desktop-app-specific frontend / IPC / Codex app-server lifecycle or request-handling problem. This is only a hypothesis. The available logs do not identify the failing message-send request or establish a root cause. Browser success makes a general account-wide outage less likely, but does not rule out all service-side or route-specific problems.

Please investigate the Linux desktop Codex path for:
- message submission and new-thread creation becoming unresponsive while history remains readable;
- the `ipc-connection-reset` event and app-server lifecycle/reconnection behavior;
- the UI remaining on the logo after relaunch instead of recovering or surfacing an error.

## Additional information

I can provide more focused, redacted journal output or repeat diagnostics if needed. Raw logs and conversation/room identifiers are intentionally omitted from this initial report.

items.body: ### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)? 26.1007.21159 (build 20052) ### What subscription do you have? ChatGPT Pro ### What platform is your computer? macOS 27.0.1 (26A434), Apple Silicon. `uname -mprs`: Darwin 27.0.0 arm64 arm. ### What issue are you seeing? Minor visual issue: clicking a noninteractive area of the conversation transcript and pressing Shift alone reveals a thin blue focus ring around the conversation pane. Portions of the outline are not visible, leaving a fragmented appearance rather than a coherent frame. The most visible sections are along the left and right edges of the pane. Chatting and keyboard navigation continue to work. This report concerns the focus indicator's presentation; it does not claim that Shift activating `:focus-visible` is itself incorrect browser behavior. ### What steps can reproduce the bug? 1. Open a conversation in the macOS desktop app, with the transcript visible. 2. Click a noninteractive area of the transcript, rather than the message input or an action button. 3. Press and release Shift alone. 4. Observe the partially visible blue outline around the conversation pane. 5. Press Tab: focus moves and the large pane outline disappears. 6. Click the transcript again and press Shift: the outline returns. ### What is the expected behavior? If a pane-wide keyboard focus ring is intentional, it should render as a coherent, clearly visible indicator around its intended bounds. Keyboard focus indication and normal Tab navigation should remain available. ### Additional information - A passive, listen-only macOS keyboard-event capture confirmed actual Left Shift input (keycode 56) directed to the app. Tab presses were captured separately as keycode 48. - Full Keyboard Access and Keyboard Navigation were disabled in the inspected macOS preferences. - Read-only inspection of the shipped bundle found the transcript component in `webview/assets/thread-scroll-layout-c566a7b214bc.js`. It makes the active transcript focusable with `tabIndex: 0` and applies `outline-none focus-visible:ring-2 focus-visible:ring-ring focus-visible:ring-inset`. The bundled CSS implements a 2-pixel inset ring. - The exact rendering layer responsible for the partially visible appearance has not been established. No app files or settings were changed during the investigation. - Related: #26160 concerned clipped focus rings in the Settings sidebar. This report concerns the conversation transcript, so it may be a separate presentation issue. ### Screenshot Screenshot from a deliberately created greeting-only demonstration conversation. items.body:
**Environment:** ChatGPT.app 26.1007.21159 (Codex Framework 155.0.8059.40), Codex Computer Use 26.1005.1001425, macOS 27.0.1, Apple Silicon (arm64).

### 1. `browser_crashpad_handler` crashes repeatedly (16 reports, Oct 3–9)
`Codex Framework.framework/Versions/155.0.8059.40/Helpers/browser_crashpad_handler`, launched by launchd, `EXC_BREAKPOINT / SIGTRAP`. Several fire within seconds of each other. Top of crashing thread:
```
logging$internal$cxxbridge1$199$init_rust_logging   (x4)
CrashpadHandlerMain
logging$internal$cxxbridge1$199$init_rust_logging
CrashpadHandlerMain
```
Rust logging init appears to trap inside the crash handler itself, so real crashes may go unreported.

### 2. `SkyComputerUseService` (Codex Computer Use) SIGSEGV null deref (4 reports) + 1 SIGABRT
`com.openai.sky.CUAService`, parent ChatGPT, `EXC_BAD_ACCESS KERN_INVALID_ADDRESS at 0x0`:
```
<null frame>
SkyComputerUseService
SkyLight (anonymous namespace)::notify_datagram_handler(...)
SkyLight CGSDatagramReadStream::dispatchMainQueueDatagrams()
CoreFoundation __CFRunLoopDoBlocks
```
A WindowServer (SkyLight) notification callback calls into a handler that is null or already released.

### 3. Agent shell PATH picks `/usr/bin/python3` (Xcode CLT Python 3.9.6) instead of Homebrew
The login shell resolves `/opt/homebrew/bin/python3` (3.14), but agent-launched commands resolve Xcode's Python 3.9.6. Scripts then stall and get killed (25 `SIGQUIT` reports from the Xcode Python, `responsibleProc: ChatGPT`). Workaround: set `PATH` under `[shell_environment_policy.set]` in `~/.codex/config.toml`. Expected: agent shells inherit the login-shell PATH, or this is documented.

Crash reports (`.ips`) available on request.

items.title: [Dots][GitHub] Size-dependent approval prompts despite "Allow all actions" (~720 KB boundary)

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: tool-calls
labels.description: Issues related to tool calling

labels.name: dots
labels.description: Issues involving setting up ChatGPT dots or managing their ongoing work.

items.body:
### What issue are you seeing?

GitHub writes involving larger file contents repeatedly request approval even though the connected GitHub plugin is configured to Allow all actions.

On October 9, 2026 (UTC), we (me and Dot) conducted controlled tests across Dot, delegated Codex workers, and scheduled tasks.

We identified a reproducible size-dependent approval pattern: 719,687-byte files succeeded without prompting, while 720,000-byte files triggered approval. The tests didn't continue to find an exact boundary between those two values.

We don't know whether this is an intentional safeguard or unexpected behavior. The issue is that unattended workflows can require additional human approval despite the user's existing authorization.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Verify execution contexts

Small GitHub file writes succeeded without approval prompting through:

- Dot directly
- A delegated Codex worker
- A scheduled task creating a file
- A scheduled task editing a file

This did not support the initial hypothesis that workers or scheduled tasks weren't inheriting permissions.

2. Test large files

We tested a JSON file containing 874,365 bytes (18,966 lines).
- Original JSON, 874,365 bytes: approval prompted.
- Minified JSON, 645,251 bytes: no prompt.
- Original JSON copied again: approval prompted.
The minified version preserved identical JSON data.

Adding one newline to each file produced the same difference: the 874,366-byte version prompted, while the 645,252-byte version did not.

3. Narrow the boundary

The underlying JSON data was kept identical while trailing whitespace varied.

Note: Value pairs are file size in bytes and whether an Approval prompt was triggered
- 700,000 No
- 715,000 No
- 718,750 No
- 719,687 No
- 720,000 Yes
- 720,625 Yes
- 722,500 Yes
- 730,000 Yes
- 760,000 Yes

The tests were conducted in a different order, progressively narrowing the boundary.

The observed transition lies above 719,687 and at or below 720,000 bytes. We didn't continue to determine the exact cutoff / boundary.

4. Check another file type

Markdown files with an ASCII heading and repeated text produced the same pattern:
- 719,687 bytes: no prompt
- 720,000 bytes: prompt

5. Compare inline content with SHA references

Additional tests using Github create_tree:

(Test; Result)
- One 645 KB file, inline content; No prompt, succeeded
- One 874 KB file, inline content; Prompt, then cancellation (Dot reported being told the user cancelled the action even though I approved the permission prompt)
- Two 645 KB files, inline content; Cancelled twice, no prompt observed -> it failed. There was no permission prompt, but Dot saw a message that the user cancelled
- Two 645 KB files, existing blob SHAs; no prompt, succeeded
- Delete both copies using tree operation; no prompt, succeeded

This demonstrates that an operation adding approximately 1.29 MB of existing content can succeed without prompting when the request references blob SHAs instead of submitting the contents inline.

6. Test incremental updates

We also tried constructing the original 874,365-byte file in two writes:
- first 437,090 bytes: no prompt
- Append the remaining 437,275 bytes: approval prompted.

The update_file operation submits the complete replacement content, so splitting the update into separate commits did not resolve the approval behavior - because the second append amounted to 874,365 bytes in total.

### What is the expected behavior?

If larger GitHub writes intentionally require additional approval despite "Allow all actions", the interface should clearly communicate this exception.

This is particularly important for Dots and scheduled tasks, where an unexpected approval requirement can interrupt unattended execution.

We're not requesting removal of legitimate security safeguards. We're asking for clarification of the expected behavior and a supported, predictable way to handle it in automated workflows.

### Additional information

**Verified workaround**

Minifying the original JSON from 874,365 to 645,251 bytes preserved its data and eliminated the prompt in the tested case.

Splitting content into separate smaller blobs and referencing their SHAs in a tree also worked. This allows a larger repository change without submitting all file contents in one operation.

However, SHA-based tree operations cannot concatenate multiple blobs into one large file.

**Evidence and limitations**

Every successful write was read back and verified.

I independently observed and reported whether an approval prompt appeared. Tool success alone was not treated as proof that approval wasn't required.

These results suggest that submitted content size matters more than total committed file size. They don't establish the internal mechanism, whether the threshold is intentional, or whether it applies to all GitHub tools.

**Related issues**

- #52503: Dots repeatedly requesting GitHub approvals
- #37184: GitHub connector ignoring persistent approval
- #48940: Authorized GitHub writes blocked by safety checks

items.title: Windows: corrupted global state resets projects and connected machines; subsequent saves overwrite fallback

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

labels.name: session
labels.description: Issues involving session (thread) management, resuming, forking, naming, archiving

items.body:
## Summary

Codex desktop lost its project sidebar and saved machine settings twice after unexpected Windows shutdowns. On the second occurrence, the app logged null-byte JSON parse failures during global-state loading. It then continued with empty state and persisted valid JSON containing no local projects or managed remote connections. The underlying SQLite database still contained 26 project records.

The user did not perform an import or enable sync before the second occurrence. A manual recovery on October 8 restored the projects; the state was lost again on October 9.

## Environment

- Windows desktop, x64, local execution.
- Second occurrence: installed package `OpenAI.Codex_26.1007.2314.0_x64`.
- Earlier recovery: package `26.1002.7124.0`.
- User state: `~/.codex/.codex-global-state.json` and `.json.bak`.
- Project database: `~/.codex/state_5.sqlite`.
- Times below use America/New_York, EDT (UTC-04:00).

## Observed timeline

| Local time | Evidence |
| --- | --- |
| October 8, morning | Windows recorded unexpected shutdowns. User reported a corrupted `config.toml` and missing sidebar projects. |
| October 8, 10:21 AM | Codex startup logged `Local app-server project migration completed projectCount=23` following manual recovery. |
| October 9, 12:37 PM | Codex startup logged `projectCount=26`. |
| October 9, 1:16:33 PM | Previous shutdown time reported by Windows EventLog 6008. |
| October 9, 1:20:09 PM | Windows Kernel-Power 41 records a reboot without a clean shutdown. |
| October 9, 1:22:05 PM | Paired `[global-state] Failed to load global state` warnings: `Unexpected token '\u0000' ... is not valid JSON`. |
| October 9, 1:22:06 PM | Local app-server migration still reports `projectCount=26`. |
| October 9, evening | App project-list API returns `projects: []`. Current state and fallback parse successfully but contain zero local projects and zero managed remote connections. Database still contains 26 projects. |

Representative logs, shortened to exclude stack paths:

```text
2026-10-09T17:22:05.892Z warning [global-state] Failed to load global state
  errorMessage="Unexpected token '\u0000', ... is not valid JSON"
2026-10-09T17:22:05.893Z warning [global-state] Failed to load global state
  errorMessage="Unexpected token '\u0000', ... is not valid JSON"
2026-10-09T17:22:06.889Z info [host-app-server-projects]
  Local app-server project migration completed projectCount=26
```

## Installed-code inspection and isolated reproduction

The installed desktop bundle's `startup-requirements-C6B1x9gL.js` contains this recovery/persistence behavior, paraphrased:

```text
load(primary):
    attempt to parse primary
    if failed, attempt to parse primary + ".bak"
    if both failed, return an empty Map

persist(state):
    serialize the current state
    write temporary file, rename over primary
    write another temporary file, rename over primary + ".bak"
```

The inspected write functions use `writeFile`/`writeFileSync` followed by rename. They do not explicitly request flushing/syncing in those functions. This is a durability concern to investigate, not proof of the original corruption cause.

An isolated test executed the extracted loader and persistence functions against synthetic local files:

1. Null-byte primary plus valid backup: the backup is successfully loaded.
2. Null-byte primary plus null-byte backup: two parse warnings are emitted and the loader returns an empty Map.
3. Add a new-session marker and call the extracted persistence function: both files become valid JSON containing only the new state. Missing project data is absent from both copies.

This reproduces the fallback/reset behavior. It does **not** reproduce power-loss corruption or prove what initially wrote the null bytes. The original corrupted files had already been replaced when evidence was collected.

## Expected behavior

Preserve corrupt originals for diagnosis; avoid silently making an empty state the only primary and backup. Keep a verified historical copy independent of the latest save, show a recovery notice, and consider repopulating local projects from surviving app-server database records.

## Actual impact

- Project sidebar is empty while the database still contains the projects.
- Saved machine entries/settings disappear while SSH configuration and referenced key files remain present.
- Latest automatic backup contains the same reset state, so restarting does not restore the projects.
- Manual recovery is possible from a separate snapshot plus database project records.

## Relevant Windows evidence and limitations

Windows recorded an unexpected shutdown directly before the second failure. The filtered October 8–9 System log also contains corrected processor hardware errors (WHEA 19, mostly internal parity errors, processor APIC ID 32). These are relevant confounding factors; they do not prove a Codex-only cause or that the CPU caused this particular file corruption. No disk/NTFS/storage-controller error entries were found in the inspected provider/time filter. No Codex/ChatGPT Application 1000/1001 crash records were found in that filter.

Windows System event 1001 separately records an earlier October 9 bugcheck `0x0000000A`, with a reboot at 12:32 PM. The 1:20 PM Kernel-Power event preceding the state-load failure has `BugcheckCode=0`, which means no bugcheck code was recorded there; it does not identify the reason for that shutdown.

Please investigate crash durability and recovery independently of the initial hardware/power-loss trigger.


## Platform readback

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26300.0 x64

## Related reports

- https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/46987 — similar null-byte state loss with surviving SQLite/session data.
- https://github.com/openai/codex/issues/44999 — separate truncated temporary global-state writes; same cause is not established.

This report adds the October 9 shutdown correlation and an isolated test of the installed primary/fallback persistence functions. Sanitized state hashes, event records, and longer log excerpts are retained locally and can be provided if requested.

### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

`26.1007.21159` (build `20052`). The bundle on this Mac is `ChatGPT.app`.

### What subscription do you have?

ChatGPT Pro.

### What platform is your computer?

`Darwin 27.0.0 arm64 arm`

The same failure also appears on a second Mac and on a Windows PC signed into the same account.

### What issue are you seeing?

The desktop cannot register this computer for a dot’s local work. The profile row shows “您的计算机 / 连接不可用” (“Your computer / Connection unavailable”). The stored error is:

`Local Work executor registration failed (HTTP 409)`

The client keeps only the status code. Replaying the same registration request returns:

`{"detail":"Maximum number of local executor registrations reached"}`

The account already has 32 local-executor records and none of them is attached: 25 named `Mac-mini.local` and 7 named `Windows`. This Mac’s registration name, `MacBook-Air.local`, is not among them. The cloud computer stays connected. This failure is only the local-executor quota.

Because registration never succeeds, this install has no local environment id, so the row has no “Allow access” control and no “Revoke access” item. On the one machine whose executor is online, its menu lists every duplicate with an empty checkbox, and Revoke is still absent because nothing is attached. Disconnecting one record returns success, and the record remains. The clear-all registration call returns 403, “OpenAI employee access required”.

The local installation id file has not changed since 2026-10-01 00:18:06 local time (mode `0600`, SHA-256 `4d6b718a52fcfd18dd25122ede294a4892c0818214bde024bd846ea68b8a065a`). The same 409 appears in desktop logs from 2026-10-02 through 2026-10-10. There is no “Local Work executor spawned” line.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. Use a ChatGPT account that already has many stale local-executor registrations.
2. Open the current Codex / ChatGPT desktop app on a computer that has not successfully registered.
3. Open the dot’s computer list, or just launch the app and let it register on startup.
4. The new computer stays on “Connection unavailable” with HTTP 409. There is no control that deletes the old registrations or frees a slot.

### What is the expected behavior?

A person can remove stale local-executor registrations, or a new registration for this installation replaces the old one, so the computer can be granted local access. The in-app error should include the server’s “maximum number of local executor registrations reached” detail. Help Center text for Allow access, Revoke access, and Offline does not mention this cap or a way to clear it.

### Additional information

No open issue matches this quota failure. #50034 has the same client string with HTTP 403 from a Cloudflare challenge. #28862 is a different 409, “Remote app server already online”. #49423 and #51735 happen after a computer is already connected.

items.title: Migrate the Windows MXC sandbox to split MXC crates
items.body:
Migrate the Windows MXC sandbox to split MXC crates

## Why

PSEC API symbols can be present on transitional Windows builds where MXC is not enabled. Availability detection needs to verify that a native process security environment can actually be created.

## What changed

- Replace `mxc-sdk` with pinned `appcontainer_common`, `learning_mode_windows`, and `wxc_common` dependencies, and update Cargo and Bazel dependency metadata.
- Use MXC's cached create/close probe for `is_available()` and query native deny-path support through `SecurityEnvironmentApi` before launching requests with denied paths.
- Adapt request construction and the existing policy test to the vector-based environment field, and update the sandbox documentation.

items.title: Codex App: an active /goal starves the external queue; codex queue items wait for a manual Steer

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

labels.name: app-server
labels.description: Issues involving app server protocol or interfaces

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From “About Codex” dialog)?

Codex App 26.1002.7124.0 (Windows package `OpenAI.Codex`). The bundled CLI reports `codex-cli 0.160.1`.

### What subscription do you have?

Not recorded; the behaviour does not depend on the plan.

### What platform is your computer?

Windows 11 Pro (10.0.26200), x64.

### What issue are you seeing?

While a thread is running a `/goal`, a message added from outside with `codex queue --thread <id> --message "…"` is not delivered at the next turn boundary. It waits until the user presses **Steer**.

From reading the installed build's app-server schema, `codex queue` maps to `thread/queue/add`, and the item is stored in `~/.codex/queue_1.sqlite`. The Desktop drains the queue (`thread/queue/start`) only while the thread is idle. Under an active goal, the goal's continuation turn starts about 64 ms after `task_complete`, so the thread is almost never idle and the queue usually loses that race. In our observations one boundary out of three went to the queue; the other two started the continuation. The queued item then sits behind every following continuation turn.

Two things make this hard to work around:

- `codex queue` exits 0 once the item is stored, so the sender cannot tell "stored" from "taken".
- `turn/steer {threadId, input, expectedTurnId}` exists, but only on the app-server that owns the thread. When the Desktop owns it, that server is its private stdio child, so no external process can reach it.

The result: a local tool that runs a long task and wakes the agent with `codex queue` when the task ends works in an ordinary thread, but stalls a goal-mode thread until a person clicks.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. In the Codex App, start a thread and run `/goal <any multi-turn goal>`.
2. While the goal is active, from a terminal run `codex queue --thread <that thread id> --message "ping"`. The command exits 0.
3. Watch the thread across several goal turns. The queued message is not taken at the boundaries; it remains queued (a row stays in `~/.codex/queue_1.sqlite`) until **Steer** is pressed.

### What is the expected behavior?

Any one of these would solve it:

1. The queue is drained at a goal's turn boundary before the continuation turn starts, or a queued item interrupts the continuation; or
2. `codex queue` gains a delivery mode that steers the active turn when there is one (as requested in #48928); or
3. a supported local endpoint lets an authorized client call `turn/steer` on a Desktop-owned thread (as requested in #51625).

Separately, it would help if `codex queue` reported whether the item was taken, or offered a way to read its state, so senders can say "queued" versus "delivered" truthfully.

### Additional information

Related: #48928 (steer mode for `codex queue`) and #51625 (external steering into a Desktop-owned active turn). This report adds the goal-mode case: in an ordinary thread the queue drains once the turn ends, but an active goal leaves almost no idle boundary, so the item waits indefinitely, not just behind one long turn.

Our current workaround, in the open-source project AlphaLattice (https://github.com/xinglin-li/alphalattice): under an active goal, the agent waits inside its turn on the task handle instead of ending the turn and relying on a queued wake. That costs model steps for long waits.

### What subscription do you have?

### Which IDE are you using?

Visual Studio Code (VS Code)

### What platform is your computer?

Microsoft Windows NT 10.0.26200.0 x64

### What issue are you seeing?

## Critical: Excessive Outbound Network Traffic in Codex

I am experiencing abnormally high network usage while running Codex in VS Code on Windows.

During a recent coding task involving changes to several files, approximately **2.5 GB of internet traffic** was observed.

Windows network monitoring showed that `codex.exe` was responsible for the vast majority of the measured traffic.

### Observed behavior

- Approximately **2.24 GB** attributed to `codex.exe` over a 24-hour monitoring period.
- Approximately **94%** of measured application traffic attributed to Codex.
- Windows Resource Monitor showed sustained outbound traffic of approximately **842,592 to 1,000,000 bytes/second**.
- In one observation, inbound traffic was only approximately **7,968 bytes/second**.
- High outbound traffic was also observed while Codex was investigating its own network usage.

### Local session files

Several JSONL session history files were unusually large:

- 212.91 MB
- 158.69 MB
- 123.95 MB
- 73.47 MB
- 59.51 MB

These are local file sizes, not confirmed transmitted network payload sizes.

### Configuration

- Model: `gpt-6.1-sol`
- Reasoning effort: `low`
- Service tier: `default`
- Operating system: Windows
- IDE: VS Code

### Impact

This behavior can consume multiple gigabytes of bandwidth during ordinary development workflows, creating significant costs for users with metered internet connections.

The exact root cause is unknown. Potential explanations include repeated context transmission, oversized tool outputs, retries, or abnormal background communication.

**Please investigate this as a potentially critical network usage regression.**

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open Visual Studio Code on Windows with the Codex extension installed.
2. Open an existing development project containing multiple source files (for example, a Next.js or ASP.NET Core application).
3. Start a Codex session using `gpt-6.1-sol` with reasoning effort set to `low`.
4. Ask Codex to perform a medium-complexity coding task involving several files.
5. Open Windows Resource Monitor using `resmon`.
6. Navigate to the Network tab.
7. Monitor the `codex.exe` process under "Processes with Network Activity".
8. Observe the Send (B/sec) column during task execution.
9. Compare the observed traffic with per-application network usage statistics.

## Observed Result

During my testing, outbound traffic reached approximately 1,000,000 bytes/sec and remained elevated during observation.

A recent coding task was associated with approximately 2.5 GB of overall internet consumption.

The issue was also observed during a subsequent diagnostic task.

## Reproducibility

Observed during multiple Codex operations on my machine.

I have not yet established a minimal reproduction in an empty workspace or confirmed whether the issue affects other users or extension versions.

### What is the expected behavior?

Codex should use network bandwidth efficiently and avoid unnecessary or repeated transmission of large amounts of data.

Expected behavior:

1. Network traffic should be reasonably proportional to the task being performed.
2. Unchanged source files, session history, and tool outputs should not be unnecessarily retransmitted.
3. Retries should not cause uncontrolled or excessive data transfers.
4. Idle or lightweight diagnostic operations should not generate sustained high outbound traffic without a legitimate reason.
5. Codex should provide sufficient diagnostics to identify unexpected network consumption.

For ordinary multi-file coding tasks, sustained uploads of approximately 1 MB/sec and multi-gigabyte network consumption should not occur without a clear technical justification.

Ideally, Codex should provide per-task upload/download metrics and safeguards against excessive bandwidth consumption.

### Additional information

## Additional Diagnostic Information

### Session analysis

I inspected the five largest local Codex JSONL session files.

The largest session contained:

- 693 `event_msg` records
- 542 `response_item` records
- 184 `token_usage_record` records
- 41 `turn_context` records
- 8 `world_state` records
- 3 `compacted` records

Its total size was approximately 212.91 MB.

Another session contained 4,867 `response_item` records but was only 73.47 MB, suggesting significant differences in average payload size between sessions.

### Network observations

Windows Resource Monitor showed substantially higher outbound than inbound traffic for `codex.exe`.

The high upload rate was observed not only during coding but also while Codex was analyzing the network consumption issue.

### Available evidence

I can provide:

- Windows Resource Monitor screenshots
- Per-application network usage screenshots
- Aggregated session statistics
- Sanitized diagnostic logs

I have not confirmed whether the traffic results from repeated context transmission, retries, tool outputs, or another internal mechanism.

### Requested engineering investigation

Please investigate possible network traffic regressions involving:

- Request payload generation
- Session history and context management
- Repeated tool-output transmission
- Retry behavior
- Background communication
- Windows-specific extension/runtime behavior

Please also consider introducing per-session network traffic diagnostics and bandwidth usage monitoring.

This issue is particularly serious for users with limited or metered internet connections.

**I request prioritization and escalation to the Codex engineering team.**

items.title: Retry bootstrap GETs through the system proxy after request failures
items.body:
Retry bootstrap GETs through the system proxy after request failures

## Why

Account discovery and cloud configuration GETs can fail after connecting but before receiving response headers. These request failures previously bypassed system proxy fallback.

## What changed

Allow bootstrap GETs to retry through the system proxy on request errors, alongside the existing connection failure and timeout cases, when fallback is enabled.

## Testing

Add regression coverage for connections closed before response headers on `accounts/check` and `config/bundle`, verifying successful proxy retries with the original request headers. Extend coverage to ensure HTTP responses with status `401`, `403`, `407`, `429`, or `503` do not trigger fallback, and network policy denials prevent requests to both the origin and proxy.

Not independently confirmed for this incident.

### What platform is your computer?

macOS 27.0.1 (Golden Gate), Apple Silicon / arm64. Exact `uname -mprs` output not collected.

### What issue are you seeing?

On **October 9, 2026**, an assistant finished a long answer in an existing conversation, but **the entire assistant message was absent from the Codex/macOS desktop chat transcript**. The UI showed only the thinking/execution-duration line (`思考了 2m 39s`, “Thought for 2m 39s”), followed immediately by my next user message. There was no error or failed-generation indication.

**The same conversation on chatgpt.com displayed the missing full answer normally.** Thus the answer was generated and persisted server-side; the issue appears to concern client-side transcript rendering, hydration, or synchronization, although no root cause has been confirmed.

The missing answer was a lengthy Chinese Markdown technical review, including headings, tables and code blocks, after inspecting a GitHub repository with the GitHub connector. I subsequently asked “有答案了吗？” (“Is the answer ready?”). The next assistant response in desktop displayed correctly, saying the detailed analysis had already been delivered, but the previous long assistant response was still absent from the desktop transcript in the captured view.

**Impact:** the user cannot read or use a successfully generated answer in the desktop client, may assume generation failed, and may request the same work again. Cross-client history is inconsistent.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

This is an observed sequence, **not yet a deterministic reproducer**:

1. Open an existing ChatGPT/Codex conversation in the macOS desktop client.
2. Ask for a long, structured research/review answer involving the GitHub connector.
3. Wait until the generation/thinking stage finishes (the affected turn displayed `思考了 2m 39s`).
4. Inspect the transcript: the **assistant's answer body is absent**, leaving the duration line and then the next user message. No error banner is visible.
5. Open the **same conversation** on chatgpt.com: the original, complete answer is visible.
6. Return to desktop and send a follow-up (“Is the answer ready?”): the assistant can refer to the previous full answer, but the missing turn is not displayed in the captured desktop transcript.

Whether switching conversations, reopening the chat, or restarting the app is required to trigger or fix the behavior **has not been established**. No logs, session ID, token usage, or render traces have been collected.

### What is the expected behavior?

Once an assistant turn successfully completes and is present in the canonical conversation (as verified on chatgpt.com), the full answer must also remain readable in the macOS desktop chat transcript. A duration/thinking line must not replace or suppress the answer. If client-side message loading fails, show a recoverable error and retry rather than silently omitting the turn.

### Additional information

- **Date observed:** 2026-10-09 (Europe/Brussels).
- **Surface:** ChatGPT conversation viewed in the unified Codex/macOS desktop client (not a local CLI task).
- **Observed asymmetry:** Web shows the full completed turn; desktop omits the entire earlier turn but can show subsequent user and assistant turns.
- **Content characteristics:** lengthy Chinese Markdown response with tables and fenced code blocks; the GitHub connector was used while preparing the answer. These are contextual observations, **not an established causal trigger**.
- **Screenshot:** A screenshot of the desktop transcript was captured: the original request is followed by the “Thought for 2m 39s” line, then the follow-up user message, with no assistant reply between them. It is not publicly attached because it includes a private repository/document name; a redacted version can be provided.
- **Related open issues:** #52454 (macOS: completed reply body disappears; duration line remains while web is intact) and #52459 (macOS: intermittent disappearing replies with web unaffected). This report adds an occurrence in which the missing answer was seen only on the web and a **subsequent desktop assistant turn was rendered normally**. It is not yet known whether this shares the same root cause.

Please investigate conversation transcript rehydration/rendering of successfully completed turns in the macOS client, especially when long answers or connector-backed responses are involved.

items.title: Windows: Docker Desktop crashes when started by Codex Desktop - agent shell runs inside MSIX AppData virtualisation (error 1920 on AF_UNIX sockets)

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

items.body:
### What version of the Codex App are you using (From "About Codex" dialog)?

26.1002.7124.0 (MSIX package `OpenAI.Codex_2p2nqsd0c76g0`)

### What subscription do you have?

Pro

### What platform is your computer?

Windows 11 Enterprise 10.0.26100, x64

### What issue are you seeing?

On Windows, the Codex desktop app runs the agent's shell, and every process started from it, under the MSIX package's AppData file-system virtualisation. In that context, Windows can't open Unix-domain socket files (reparse tag `0x80000023`) under `%APPDATA%` or `%LOCALAPPDATA%`. Rename and delete fail with `ERROR_CANT_ACCESS_FILE` (1920, "The file cannot be accessed by the system"). Processes outside the package context open the same files normally.

**Impact:** Docker Desktop started by the agent crashes on every start once a previous session's sockets exist:

```
rename C:/Users/<user>/AppData/Local/Docker/run/sailor-ingest.sock C:/Users/<user>/AppData/Local/Docker/run/sailor-ingest.sock.stale: The file cannot be accessed by the system.
```

Only the user sees the dialog. The agent sees `docker` failing to connect, so it retries and renames folders aside. On the affected machine, 8 copies of Docker's `docker-secrets-engine` folder had ended up in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Packages\OpenAI.Codex_2p2nqsd0c76g0\LocalCache\Local`, where nothing outside the app can see them.

**Evidence:** the full trace was captured with Claude Desktop, which is also MSIX, has the identical problem and was on the same machine.

- A Windows Performance Recorder trace shows the agent shell's AppData opens being redirected into the package's `LocalCache`.
- For the same socket file, opening it fails with error 1920 from the agent shell, and succeeds from a process started through `explorer.exe` or WMI.

### What steps can reproduce the bug?

1. From a Codex agent shell, create an AF_UNIX socket under `%APPDATA%\sock-test\` and exit without closing it, using PowerShell 7:
   ```powershell
   New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force "$env:APPDATA\sock-test" | Out-Null
   $s = [System.Net.Sockets.Socket]::new([System.Net.Sockets.AddressFamily]::Unix, [System.Net.Sockets.SocketType]::Stream, [System.Net.Sockets.ProtocolType]::Unspecified)
   $s.Bind([System.Net.Sockets.UnixDomainSocketEndPoint]::new("$env:APPDATA\sock-test\a.sock")); [Environment]::Exit(0)
   ```
2. Run `fsutil reparsepoint query "$env:APPDATA\sock-test\a.sock"` from the agent shell, then from a normal terminal.

The expected result is `Error 1920` from the agent shell and success from the normal terminal. This was verified from Claude Desktop's agent shell on the same machine. Docker Desktop started by Codex agents shows the same crash.

### What is the expected behavior?

Processes started by the agent should see and use the real AppData, the same as a normal terminal. Docker Desktop started by the agent should start normally.

### Additional information

- Related open report: #41665 describes MSIX AppData redirection. This report focuses on AF_UNIX access failures and Docker Desktop crashes.

- **Suggested fix:** start agent shell and tool processes outside the app container, for example with `PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_DESKTOP_APP_POLICY` and `PROCESS_CREATION_DESKTOP_APP_BREAKAWAY_ENABLE_PROCESS_TREE`. Alternatively, opt the package out of AppData write virtualisation.
- **Workaround:** start Docker Desktop with `explorer.exe "C:\Program Files\Docker\Docker\Docker Desktop.exe"`.
- **Versions:** Docker Desktop 4.89.0, WSL 2.7.13.0.
- **Same bug in Claude Desktop:** reported at anthropics/claude-code#73543 and anthropics/claude-code#76383. New report with the trace evidence: https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/issues/100901.

items.title: [Windows desktop 26.930.3930.0] Local project chats still fail as helpers recreate mirror folder locks

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

items.body:
## Summary

The Windows desktop app intermittently cannot start a new local Work chat in an existing project. This materially disrupts normal use across multiple projects.

This report documents a current reproduction on **OpenAI.Codex 26.930.3930.0**, observed October 9, 2026. Related reports: #44736, #45596, and #34499. This appears to be the same failure class on a later build, not a confirmed new regression.

## Environment

- Windows desktop, Microsoft Store package `OpenAI.Codex 26.930.3930.0`.
- Local Work execution.
- The user reports creating and maintaining the affected projects entirely through desktop and not opening the cloud interface in days.
- Subscription and exact Windows build were not collected.
- Project identifiers and personal filesystem paths are omitted.

## Visible error

> Could not use this project for a local chat

The screenshot shows Work selected and this error while attempting to use the affected project.

## Reproduction observed

1. Open an existing project in the Windows desktop app.
2. Attempt to start a new local Work chat.
3. The error above appears.
4. Identify and terminate only the background helpers holding the affected project mirror as their current working directory, while the visible project chats are idle.
5. Verify that a non-mutating directory rename-access probe now succeeds.
6. Retry starting a new Work chat through the normal desktop UI.
7. The same error returns. Fresh helpers again use the project mirror as their current working directory, and the directory access probe again fails.

The last retry was confirmed by the user. Successful directory access alone did **not** establish successful chat creation.

## Verified diagnostics

Desktop logs repeatedly contain:

```text
ChatGPT project context sync failed
fileOrdinal=null projectSaveCount=0 sourceCount=0
stage=filesystem status=null syncFileCount=0
```

A failure after the retry was recorded at **2026-10-09T20:14:24.531Z**.

The affected mirror is under:

```text
C:\Users\<user>\.codex\.chatgpt-projects\<project-id>
```

- A handle-only access probe using Windows `CreateFileW`, requested `DELETE` access, full read/write/delete sharing, `OPEN_EXISTING`, and `FILE_FLAG_BACKUP_SEMANTICS`. It did not rename or delete anything.
- The probe initially returned **Windows error 32**, a sharing violation.
- Six `node.exe` / `node_repl.exe` helpers had that exact mirror directory as their current working directory. The visible project chats were idle.
- After stopping the verified helpers, the identical probe succeeded.
- Following the user's failed retry, three newly observed helpers again had the same directory as their current working directory, and the probe again returned error 32.
- No project files, saved chats, signed app binaries, or application configuration were modified during this investigation.

## Installed implementation inspected

In the installed app's `.vite/build/main-C_jM0dPl.js`, the project synchronization routine stages a replacement mirror, renames the existing mirror to a previous-directory path, then renames the staged directory into place.

The UI error is emitted after project-context synchronization fails.

This strongly supports a conflict between helper working-directory handles and mirror replacement on Windows. **The exact failed filesystem syscall was not directly traced**, so attributing the logged failure specifically to the rename remains an inference supported by the implementation and sharing-violation probes.

## Expected behavior

Starting a new local Work chat should work reliably with existing project chats idle. App-managed helpers should not block project synchronization. Users should not need repeated helper termination or project-by-project repairs.

## Impact and requested investigation

This affects multiple projects and materially interferes with using the platform. Clearing the lock provides only temporary relief because helpers recreate it.

Please investigate synchronization versus helper startup/prewarming and existing-session lifecycles on Windows. A durable fix should preserve project associations and context and be validated through the normal composer across successive chats and app restarts.

Please also preserve the original filesystem error in diagnostics rather than reporting only `stage=filesystem`.

The configuration workaround described in #44736 was not applied or validated in this October 9 investigation. This report does not claim that no workaround exists, or that the underlying issue has been fixed.

items.title: [Windows Desktop] 2h34 turn with reconnects, no useful progress, then completed without confirmed recovery

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: model-behavior
labels.description: Issues related to behaviors exhibited by the model

labels.name: windows-os
labels.description: Issues related to Codex on Windows systems

labels.name: app
labels.description: Issues related to the Codex desktop app

labels.name: connectivity
labels.description: Issues involving networking or endpoint connectivity problems (disconnections)

items.body:
## Summary

On **October 9, 2026**, a long-running local software-development conversation in **Codex Desktop for Windows** had a turn lasting **2 h 34 min 20 s**. During the turn, the UI showed reconnection attempts and the monitored turn state remained `active / inProgress`, with `error: null` and no fresh useful public result. The assistant subsequently **acknowledged it had made no progress on the six requested local support functions**.

The turn ultimately ended with `status: completed` and `error: null`. The assistant said it had recovered a saved checkpoint and would continue, but **no subsequent active turn or completed deliverable was observed at the final check**. This is a *reliability/progress/recovery visibility* report, not a claim about the root cause or quota accounting.

## Environment

- Product: Codex Desktop; local Windows execution using PowerShell
- Task: implement and test six local support functions around an existing controller (checks, evidence, receipts, manifest, parent package, reports)
- Conversation: long-lived, with prior turns and saved checkpoints
- Exact Codex Desktop version / bundled runtime version: **not captured**
- Model and reasoning effort *for the affected turn*: **not verified**
- No controlled reproduction was performed

## Timeline (October 9, 2026; UTC)

| Time | Evidence / observation |
| --- | --- |
| **17:42:43** | Official affected turn start |
| ~**17:43** | Assistant publicly announced preparation and testing of six supporting functions |
| **18:49:12** | Last write time of a locally inspected `RESULT.json` checkpoint, which still recorded zero implemented support callbacks and no native launches or submissions. **Its metadata referred to an earlier turn**, so this file is *not* treated as authoritative proof of the affected turn's terminal state |
| Time not embedded in screenshot | Desktop showed **"Running for 2h 15m 21s"**, **"Reconnecting 1/5"**, then **"Reconnecting 2/5"** and **"Thinking"**; a `RESULT.json` creation was also displayed (+26 / -0). None of this proves useful task completion |
| **20:12** | Assistant publicly acknowledged a malfunction, stating (translated from French): **"I got stuck in a reasoning loop, without advancing the six support functions. No native launch or native effect was executed."** This is the assistant's characterization, **not proof of an internal reasoning-loop mechanism** |
| **20:17:03** | Official turn end: `completed`, `error: null`. Total elapsed **9,260,379 ms (2h 34m 20.379s)**, including subsequent status checking and checkpoint inspection |

During the incident, compact official observations repeatedly showed `active / inProgress` with `error: null`. Technical markers changed, but no corresponding fresh useful public output was observed. The monitor did not re-submit an already accepted continuation.

After the final response, the conversation was observed as `idle`. **An idle conversation after a final answer is not itself erroneous**; it only means that the claimed continuation/recovery was **not confirmed by observed follow-on work**.

## Expected vs actual

**Expected:** An accepted turn should either perform observable useful work, report a genuine blocker, or enter a clear bounded failure/retry state. After interruptions/reconnections, the system should distinguish *transport retries*, *model activity*, *actual tool/task progress*, and *successful recovery*. Checkpoints and previously accepted effects must be preserved without replaying already consumed native actions.

**Observed:** The turn remained active for more than two and a half hours; the assistant acknowledged no progress on the requested implementation; and the turn ended successfully according to lifecycle status, despite no verified deliverable or follow-on work at the final check.

## Impact

- Material user delay and loss of confidence in whether the long-running task is progressing
- Six requested functions not shown delivered or qualified by the collected evidence
- Inadequate user-visible distinction among ongoing activity, reconnecting, substantive progress, and recovery
- Saved checkpoint remained recoverable; no destructive recovery action was attempted by the monitoring agent

## Evidence limits / non-claims

- **No root cause established**: client, server, transport, local network, model, context length, permissions, or other factors remain possibilities
- **No confirmed regional service outage**, token/quota loss, or billable-usage attribution
- No proof that reasoning streamed continuously for the entire 2h34, nor that the agent's "reasoning loop" description is technically accurate
- Turn duration is **not** an exact measurement of time stalled
- An earlier `stream disconnected before completion: Transport error: network error: error decoding response body` happened **in a separate invocation on the same day**. It is *not* assigned as this turn's error or presumed causal
- No deterministic reproducer; exact affected app/model versions not recovered
- This public report intentionally excludes raw logs, transcript, private project context, paths, account/session/turn UUIDs, and other correlation identifiers

## Requested investigation

1. Correlate **reconnection attempts**, lifecycle `active / inProgress` and final `completed / error: null`, and the absence of verified substantive task progress.
2. Explain which signals the Desktop/app-server can expose to distinguish genuine generation, transport retry, stalled execution, and successful continuation.
3. Check whether prolonged turns can complete without making task progress after reconnect/retry episodes, and whether an explicit recoverable state or watchdog is warranted.
4. Provide a safe private route for targeted server-side correlation identifiers or redacted diagnostics, if needed.
5. Ensure recovery preserves the established checkpoint and does not re-execute effects already applied.

Potentially related, **not asserted as the same cause**:
- #37775 — multi-hour active Windows turns without useful progress
- #50086 — Windows WebSocket reconnects and misleading post-recovery response
- #52529 — Windows long-lived turns streaming reasoning without tool/task progress

_Reported at the affected account holder's request. No raw session or private project material is being shared in this issue._

labels.name: enhancement

labels.name: codex-web

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

Codex desktop app (macOS): Local and Cloud sessions. This request is specifically about **remote Cloud execution**, not local Git worktrees.

### What feature would you like to see?

**Make a Google Drive folder a first-class, durable Codex Cloud project workspace, with native bidirectional handoff to local files—without requiring a GitHub repository or an always-on computer.**

#### Real workflow

- I use Google Drive for desktop in **mirrored** mode on both a MacBook and a Mac mini.
- My project folders and day-to-day work already live in Google Drive. The same project files are available on both Macs.
- Codex Local can work in these folders while a Mac is running.
- For longer tasks, I want to switch the *same project* to Codex Cloud, close both Macs, and have Codex work on OpenAI-hosted infrastructure.
- When the task finishes, its changes should appear automatically in the **same Google Drive folder**, and subsequently on each Mac through the normal Google Drive sync.

Today, the cloud flow is primarily tied to GitHub repository environments. Moving files into GitHub, pushing/pulling, configuring custom Drive APIs or `rclone`, or setting up a GitHub-to-Drive export pipeline is unnecessary overhead for people whose canonical workspace is already Google Drive.

#### Proposed user experience

```
Codex project: [Google Drive > My Drive > selected folder]
Execution:     [Local] [Cloud]
                              ↓
              Codex runs remotely; Macs can be off
                              ↓
                 Changes saved to same Drive folder
                              ↓
              Existing Google Drive desktop mirror syncs
                  to MacBook and Mac mini normally
```

Requested capabilities:

1. **Cloud workspace picker:** authorize Google Drive and select an existing folder as the project root; do not require a GitHub repo.
2. **Remote execution:** snapshot/materialize the selected Drive folder into an isolated cloud working directory. Cloud tasks run even when local computers are offline.
3. **Native write-back:** safely publish changed files to that same Drive folder automatically, preserving paths and file formats. Show which changes were written and when.
4. **Seamless Local ↔ Cloud handoff:** use the same logical project identity and source files across MacBook, Mac mini and hosted tasks. No manual export/import, repository migration or custom integration.
5. **Safe reconciliation:** detect concurrent edits via revision IDs/ETags, avoid silent overwrites, show conflicts, and support revision recovery/rollback and clear sync failure notices.
6. **Efficient sync:** transfer changed durable project files, not high-churn temporary build outputs, dependency caches, Git internals or other ephemeral artifacts by default. Run heavy builds in the cloud sandbox rather than directly inside the Drive sync folder.
7. **Scoped security:** OAuth with least-privilege access to the chosen folder; clear read/write scopes and access revocation; do not inject Drive credentials into shell sessions.
8. **Optional Git:** people who need GitHub and PRs should keep those workflows. Git version control should not be a prerequisite for folder-based cloud tasks.

**Minimum viable version:** choose a Drive folder → start Cloud task → fetch its files to hosted workspace → show/publish a file-level change set back to Drive safely → reopen locally from the original synced folder.

### Why this matters

Cloud execution solves an important problem: the computer can be turned off while substantial Codex work continues. For users whose primary storage is a synced folder rather than a GitHub repo, that benefit is diminished by the need for repo migration or bespoke synchronization. This affects solo developers, prototypers, creative-technical projects, and mixed code/document/asset workflows.

This request is **not** just:
- importing a Google Doc into task context;
- exposing a Google Drive connector as a callable tool;
- downloading one Drive artifact;
- configuring a GitHub → Drive mirror;
- syncing Codex chat history between devices.

It is about Google Drive as **the canonical persistent project workspace** with an ordinary local/cloud execution toggle.

### Related information

- #38821 — Google Drive connector/tools unavailable in delegated cloud tasks (related, not equivalent).
- #50277 — reliable Drive artifact import (one-way import, not persistent two-way workspace).
- #28729 — cloud-sync safety risks from build caches/other high-churn files; suggests the cloud build sandbox + selective durable artifact write-back design.
  
Would the Codex team consider adding this as a workspace backend, potentially extensible later to OneDrive/Dropbox?

items.body:
### What variant of Codex are you using?

ChatGPT dot in the mobile app.

### What feature would you like to see?

Please let dot initiate an actual incoming voice call when something important needs my attention.

Ordinary notifications are easy to miss in notification overload, especially for people who keep their phones on silent. If dot notices a genuinely important, time-sensitive update, it should have the option to call and explain what needs attention.

Requested behavior:
- An opt-in setting allowing dot to call for important alerts, with simple controls for when it can call.
- A real incoming-call screen with answer and decline controls.
- On answering, dot briefly explains why it called and lets the conversation continue naturally.
- If the call is missed or declined, leave a concise summary in the dot conversation.

Examples could include a last-minute change affecting an upcoming plan, an approaching deadline that needs a decision, or a task blocked on an urgent answer.

### Additional information

Please make it clear how these calls interact with silent mode and Do Not Disturb on each platform, including any supported settings users would need to enable.
